title: Proxy Pattern
summary: A stand-in that controls access to a real object — lazily, securely, or across the network — while looking exactly like the real thing to callers.

slides.markdown:
A **Proxy** is a stand-in object that implements the same interface as a real object and controls access to it — lazily creating it, checking permissions before forwarding, or hiding the fact that it lives on another machine.

Think of a building receptionist: visitors don't walk straight to an executive's office, they go through the receptionist first, who decides whether and when to let them through. Callers of a proxy don't know — and shouldn't need to know — whether they're talking to the real object or a stand-in.

slides.sectionTitle: Proxy: a stand-in that controls access to a real object
slides.markdown:
A **Proxy** implements the exact same interface as a real object (the *real subject*) but doesn't do the real work itself — it holds a reference to the real subject and decides whether, when, and how a call actually reaches it. The caller has no way to tell, from the interface alone, whether it's talking to the real object or a stand-in.

That single fact — same interface, extra decision-making in front — is what lets a proxy add lazy creation, permission checks, caching, or network indirection without the caller's code changing at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Virtual proxy (lazy loading), protection proxy (access control), remote proxy (network)
slides.markdown:
Proxies come in three common flavors, solving different access problems with the same shape. A **virtual proxy** delays creating an expensive object until needed — a `LazyImage` that doesn't decode the file until `.render()` is called. A **protection proxy** checks permissions before forwarding — an `AdminActionProxy` that verifies a role before `deleteUser()` reaches the real service. A **remote proxy** makes a call to another process look local — an RPC stub that looks like a normal method call but actually serializes a network request.

All three share one shape: same interface as the real object, extra logic before delegating.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a caching proxy in front of an expensive ImageLoader
Compare: Proxy vs Decorator — controlling access vs adding behavior
slides.markdown:
Structurally near-identical to Decorator — same interface, holds a reference, delegates — but the intent differs.

| | Proxy | Decorator |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Control or optimize access to the real object | Add a new responsibility to the object |
| Typical caller awareness | Often invisible — caller doesn't know a proxy exists | Deliberate — caller explicitly chooses to stack it |
| Adds new capability? | No — same capability, gated or optimized | Yes — the object can now do something new |
| Example | Lazy loading, permission checks, RPC stubs | Compression, encryption, logging |

**How to decide:** if you're deciding whether/when a call reaches the real object, it's Proxy; if you're deciding what extra happens once it does, see [Decorator](decorator-pattern).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a proxy that silently changes semantics the client depends on, e.g. hidden latency
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A proxy is transparent, so it can't change how the client's code behaves."

**Why it's wrong:** a remote proxy that makes a network call look local hides real semantic changes — the call can now fail from a timeout, arrive out of order, or take 200ms instead of 200ns. Code written assuming a cheap, always-succeeding local call — looping over it thousands of times — can silently become a performance or reliability disaster.

**Correct model:** transparency of interface doesn't mean transparency of cost or failure mode. Document what a proxy can fail or slow down on, and design callers with timeouts and backoff where it hides a genuinely remote or expensive operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up: lazy-loaded ORM associations, RPC stubs
slides.markdown:
ORMs use virtual proxies constantly: accessing `user.orders` may return a proxy that only queries the database when you actually iterate over it, not when `User` loads — this is exactly why the N+1 query problem happens, since each access can silently trigger its own query. gRPC and other RPC frameworks generate remote-proxy stubs that look like local method calls but serialize arguments over the network.

**When NOT to use it:** if the extra indirection makes reasoning about the real object's lifecycle genuinely harder, and the object isn't actually expensive or remote, a direct reference is simpler.
